extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists (especially gag/cartoonists submitting to The New Yorker) practicing weekly batch production and submission
extracted.subtask_description: Craft and submit weekly batches of gag cartoons for magazines like The New Yorker, emphasizing caption-first writing, high-volume idea generation, tight drawing that serves the gag, and editorial fit. Focus is on a disciplined weekly production workflow and criteria that increase likelihood of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly batch-production discipline / submission volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoonists submit ~10 cartoons per week to The New Yorker; most weeks, zero are bought. The discipline is to keep producing despite zero feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a high cadence (weekly batches) to stay in practice and develop material; repeated submission helps develop relationships with editors. Accept that rejection is the norm and the goal is sustained output rather than immediate validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate 30+ premises to produce the strongest 10
rubrics_metrics.description: Rosen's working method: brainstorm 30+ premises, draw the strongest 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat idea generation as a numbers game—most premises will be bad; only a few will survive. Use aggressive brainstorming to surface the few workable premises worth drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise originality (not recently seen in the magazine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the premise original (not seen in this magazine recently)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source premises from news headlines, literalizing idioms, animals doing human things, or collisions of unrelated tropes. Check recent issues for repetition; editorial selection favors ideas that feel new to the magazine's pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing serves the gag (avoid overdrawn work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in drawing is necessary but not sufficient—the drawing must serve the gag; overdrawn cartoons distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity and economy of line. Remove visual clutter that competes with the joke. Use drawing to deliver the punchline rather than to show off technical prowess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negative space to aid caption reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative space gives the eye time to read the caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose panels so the eye rests and the caption can be read easily; excessive detail around the caption area can impede the joke's reception. Negative space is a deliberate tool to pace reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption-first working method (Rosen's preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rosen advocates caption-first: comedy lives in the language; image executes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cartoonists generate captions in batches and then sketch images; others sketch first. Rosen recommends writing the caption (the linguistic gag) first, then designing an image that executes it cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption length constraint (under 12 words)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caption you can't get under 12 words probably isn't ready. Strive for brevity so the gag reads sharply; long captions indicate the joke needs tightening or reworking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image–caption lock works 'cold' (immediately understandable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the lock between image and caption work cold?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relationship between image and caption should make sense instantly without additional explanation. If the gag requires context or protracted set-up, it won't read well in the single-panel magazine format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing when to quit / three-draw rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A cartoon you can't draw clean in three tries probably isn't ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you fail to render the gag clearly after a few attempts, move on—salvage the premise later. Iteration is useful, but persistent inability to make the image work is a stop condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor selection criteria: originality, tonal fit, drawable into the magazine
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor selects ~17 of ~1000 weekly submissions. Selection criteria: original, tonal fit, drawable into the magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether your joke matches the magazine's sensibility (tone) and whether it can be executed simply and recognizably in the magazine's single-panel format. Editorial fit often outweighs technical polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce weekly enough to stay loose
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you producing weekly enough to stay loose?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular weekly practice keeps ideas and execution flexible. Frequency of production is a metric of health for a cartoonist's pipeline and creativity: infrequent work reduces looseness and idea flow.
